reference.title: Visual reference: yourgenome · From DNA to protein – 3D

captions.text: Inside a cell, molecular machines turn genetic information into proteins.
The nucleus contains DNA. We move from the whole cell toward its genetic material.
A chromosome illustrates DNA packaging; active genes are read from less condensed chromatin.
DNA wraps around histone proteins. Unpacking reveals the double helix.
A gene is a region of DNA whose sequence carries instructions.
RNA polymerase binds DNA and opens a small transcription bubble.
One DNA strand serves as the template for a complementary RNA copy.
Incoming RNA bases pair with the template: A with U, and G with C.
Each new nucleotide extends the RNA at its 3′ end. The DNA is retained.
The RNA transcript separates from its template. Processing is omitted in this overview.
Messenger RNA passes through a nuclear pore into the cytoplasm.
A ribosome assembles around the RNA to read its sequence.
A transfer RNA carries an amino acid. This cloverleaf is a simplified structural diagram.
Its anticodon pairs with a complementary three-base codon in the messenger RNA.
The growing peptide transfers to the amino acid on the incoming transfer RNA.
The ribosome advances by one codon. The empty transfer RNA leaves, and the cycle repeats.
The connected chain of amino acids emerges from the ribosome.
After release, the chain folds into a compact three-dimensional protein.
These shapes and times are schematic; they illustrate the mechanism, not atomistic dynamics.
